17. Law of Large Numbers¶

For IID variables with finite mean (\mu), the sample average

[ \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i ]

moves toward (\mu).

The Weak Law states

[ P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\epsilon)\to0. ]

The Strong Law gives almost-sure convergence under suitable assumptions.

LLN: stability of averages¶

The Law of Large Numbers explains why repeated sampling makes averages stable.

For IID observations with suitable finite expectation,

[ \bar X_n\to\mu. ]

The important point is not that individual observations become less random. They do not. Instead, positive and negative deviations increasingly balance in the average.

The Weak Law describes shrinking probability of a fixed error; the Strong Law describes pathwise convergence with probability one.

Scenario 17A — Exponential sample means concentrate around the true mean¶

Recognition pattern¶

Exponential models waiting time to the next event when events follow a constant-rate Poisson process.

Its constant hazard and memorylessness are two views of the same underlying lack-of-ageing property.

In [47]:
plots=[]
R=4000
for n in [5,20,100,1000]:
    means=rng.exponential(scale=1,size=(R,n)).mean(axis=1)
    p=bokeh_hist(means,60,True,f'Distribution of sample mean, n={n}','sample mean')
    p.add_layout(Span(location=1,dimension='height',line_dash='dashed',line_width=2))
    plots.append(p)
show(column(*plots))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

Increasing sample size stabilises averages because independent deviations are increasingly averaged out. The individual observations remain random; what becomes stable is the aggregate.

Checkpoint: state the difference between convergence of the sample mean and convergence of the underlying observations.

Scenario 17B — Weak Law in probability form¶

For fixed (\epsilon=0.15), estimate

[ P(|\bar X_n-1|>0.15). ]

What the experiment measures¶

Fix an error tolerance (\epsilon). For each (n), repeatedly generate a sample and compute (\bar X_n). Then estimate

[ P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\epsilon). ]

The Weak Law predicts this probability approaches zero as (n) grows.

In [48]:
eps=0.15
ns=np.array([5,10,20,50,100,200,500,1000])
R=5000
probs=[]
for n in ns:
    means=rng.exponential(scale=1,size=(R,n)).mean(axis=1)
    probs.append(np.mean(np.abs(means-1)>eps))
source=ColumnDataSource({'n':ns,'prob':probs})
p=figure(title='Weak Law: probability of fixed estimation error',width=800,height=420,
         x_axis_type='log',x_axis_label='Sample size n',y_axis_label='P(|mean-μ|>ε)',
         tools='pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save')
r=p.line('n','prob',source=source,line_width=3)
p.scatter('n','prob',source=source,size=8)
p.add_tools(HoverTool(renderers=[r],tooltips=[('n','@n'),('probability','@prob{0.0000}')]))
show(p)

Interpretation and takeaway¶

Increasing sample size stabilises averages because independent deviations are increasingly averaged out. The individual observations remain random; what becomes stable is the aggregate.

Checkpoint: state the difference between convergence of the sample mean and convergence of the underlying observations.

Scenario 17C — Strong Law intuition through sample paths¶

How to interpret sample paths¶

Each curve is one infinite-sequence idea truncated to a finite simulation. At small (n), the running average can move dramatically. As more observations accumulate, each new observation has weight only (1/n), so the path stabilises near (\mu).

In [85]:
nmax=5000
p=figure(title='Running means for exponential sample paths',width=850,height=430,
         x_axis_type='log',x_axis_label='n',y_axis_label='Running sample mean',
         tools='pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save')
for i in range(6):
    x=rng.exponential(scale=1,size=nmax)
    running=np.cumsum(x)/np.arange(1,nmax+1)
    p.line(np.arange(1,nmax+1),running,line_width=1.5,legend_label=f'Path {i+1}')
p.add_layout(Span(location=1,dimension='width',line_dash='dashed',line_width=3))
p.legend.click_policy='hide'
show(p)

Interpretation and takeaway¶

Increasing sample size stabilises averages because independent deviations are increasingly averaged out. The individual observations remain random; what becomes stable is the aggregate.

Checkpoint: state the difference between convergence of the sample mean and convergence of the underlying observations.

Scenario 17D — When the mean does not exist: Cauchy averages¶

A standard Cauchy distribution has no finite mean. Its running average does not stabilise the way the previous LLN examples do.

This is a reminder that theorem assumptions matter.

Why this counterexample matters¶

The Cauchy distribution has no finite expectation or variance. Its extreme values are influential enough that averages do not settle the way they do under ordinary LLN/CLT assumptions.

This is a reminder to read theorem assumptions before applying theorem conclusions.

In [86]:
nmax=5000
p=figure(title='Cauchy running averages: no stable population mean',width=850,height=430,
         x_axis_type='log',x_axis_label='n',y_axis_label='Running average',
         tools='pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save')
for i in range(4):
    x=rng.standard_cauchy(size=nmax)
    running=np.cumsum(x)/np.arange(1,nmax+1)
    p.line(np.arange(1,nmax+1),np.clip(running,-20,20),line_width=1.5,legend_label=f'Path {i+1}')
p.legend.click_policy='hide'
show(p)

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The numerical output is a finite-sample approximation to the theoretical probability result. Small differences are expected.

When interpreting a simulation, always separate:

  • the theorem or exact formula,
  • the estimator used in the code,
  • finite-simulation error,
  • and the visual evidence.

18. Central Limit Theorem¶

For IID variables with finite mean (\mu) and variance (\sigma^2),

[ Z_n=\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1). ]

The parent population does not need to be Normal.

CLT: shape of sampling uncertainty¶

The CLT answers a different question from the LLN.

  • LLN: Where does (\bar X_n) go? Toward (\mu).
  • CLT: What does the properly rescaled error around (\mu) look like? Approximately Normal.

[ \frac{\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)}{\sigma} \xrightarrow{d}N(0,1). ]

The (1/\sqrt n) scale is fundamental: typical estimation error shrinks proportionally to (1/\sqrt n), not (1/n).

Scenario 18A — CLT from an Exponential population¶

The Exponential population is strongly skewed, making convergence visually obvious.

Recognition pattern¶

Exponential models waiting time to the next event when events follow a constant-rate Poisson process.

Its constant hazard and memorylessness are two views of the same underlying lack-of-ageing property.

In [87]:
R=8000
grid=np.linspace(-4,4,500)
plots=[]
for n in [1,2,5,10,30,100]:
    data=rng.exponential(scale=1,size=(R,n))
    z=np.sqrt(n)*(data.mean(axis=1)-1)
    p=bokeh_hist(z,70,True,f'CLT from Exponential population, n={n}','standardised mean')
    p.line(grid,stats.norm.pdf(grid),line_width=3,legend_label='N(0,1)')
    p.x_range.start=-4; p.x_range.end=4
    plots.append(p)
show(column(*plots))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

As sample size grows, the standardised sampling distribution should become more Normal, provided the relevant CLT assumptions hold.

Do not conclude that the raw observations become Normal. The CLT concerns a properly standardised aggregate such as the sample mean.

Checkpoint: distinguish the role of (n), (\mu), (\sigma), and the (\sqrt n) scaling.

Scenario 18B — CLT for Bernoulli sample proportions¶

For Bernoulli data, the sample mean is a sample proportion. The CLT gives

[ \frac{\hat p-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}\approx N(0,1). ]

Recognition pattern¶

Use Bernoulli when there is one binary outcome.

Code often represents the two outcomes as 1 and 0. This makes expectation especially intuitive:

[ E[X]=1\cdot p+0\cdot(1-p)=p. ]

So the mean of many Bernoulli observations is exactly the observed success proportion.

In [52]:
p0=0.2
R=8000
plots=[]
for n in [10,30,100,500]:
    x=rng.binomial(1,p0,size=(R,n))
    phat=x.mean(axis=1)
    z=(phat-p0)/np.sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n)
    p=bokeh_hist(z,60,True,f'Bernoulli CLT, n={n}','standardised proportion')
    p.line(grid,stats.norm.pdf(grid),line_width=3,legend_label='N(0,1)')
    p.x_range.start=-4; p.x_range.end=4
    plots.append(p)
show(column(*plots))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

As sample size grows, the standardised sampling distribution should become more Normal, provided the relevant CLT assumptions hold.

Do not conclude that the raw observations become Normal. The CLT concerns a properly standardised aggregate such as the sample mean.

Checkpoint: distinguish the role of (n), (\mu), (\sigma), and the (\sqrt n) scaling.

Scenario 18C — CLT from a strongly skewed Lognormal population¶

A highly skewed parent distribution generally needs larger (n) before the Normal approximation looks convincing.

Standardisation step by step¶

Subtracting (\mu) recentres the variable at zero. Dividing by (\sigma) expresses distance in units of standard deviations:

[ Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}. ]

This transformation allows all Normal probability calculations to be reduced to the standard Normal distribution.

In [53]:
sigma_ln=1.2
mu_ln=0
true_mean=np.exp(mu_ln+sigma_ln**2/2)
true_var=(np.exp(sigma_ln**2)-1)*np.exp(2*mu_ln+sigma_ln**2)
true_sd=np.sqrt(true_var)
plots=[]
for n in [5,30,100,500]:
    x=rng.lognormal(mu_ln,sigma_ln,size=(6000,n))
    z=np.sqrt(n)*(x.mean(axis=1)-true_mean)/true_sd
    p=bokeh_hist(z,70,True,f'Lognormal CLT, n={n}','standardised mean')
    p.line(grid,stats.norm.pdf(grid),line_width=3,legend_label='N(0,1)')
    p.x_range.start=-4; p.x_range.end=4
    plots.append(p)
show(column(*plots))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

As sample size grows, the standardised sampling distribution should become more Normal, provided the relevant CLT assumptions hold.

Do not conclude that the raw observations become Normal. The CLT concerns a properly standardised aggregate such as the sample mean.

Checkpoint: distinguish the role of (n), (\mu), (\sigma), and the (\sqrt n) scaling.

Scenario 18D — Classical CLT failure: Cauchy sample means¶

The finite-variance CLT does not apply to Cauchy variables. In fact, an average of IID standard Cauchy variables is still Cauchy distributed.

Why this counterexample matters¶

The Cauchy distribution has no finite expectation or variance. Its extreme values are influential enough that averages do not settle the way they do under ordinary LLN/CLT assumptions.

This is a reminder to read theorem assumptions before applying theorem conclusions.

In [54]:
plots=[]
for n in [1,5,30,100]:
    x=rng.standard_cauchy(size=(5000,n))
    means=x.mean(axis=1)
    means=means[np.abs(means)<20]
    p=bokeh_hist(means,80,True,f'Cauchy sample mean, n={n}','sample mean')
    p.x_range.start=-10; p.x_range.end=10
    plots.append(p)
show(column(*plots))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

As sample size grows, the standardised sampling distribution should become more Normal, provided the relevant CLT assumptions hold.

Do not conclude that the raw observations become Normal. The CLT concerns a properly standardised aggregate such as the sample mean.

Checkpoint: distinguish the role of (n), (\mu), (\sigma), and the (\sqrt n) scaling.

Scenario 18E — Quantify convergence with the KS statistic¶

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic measures discrepancy from (N(0,1)). Smaller is closer.

Student workflow¶

Before running the code:

  1. identify the random experiment,
  2. state the relevant random variable/event,
  3. write the theoretical quantity being estimated,
  4. predict the qualitative plot shape,
  5. run the simulation,
  6. explain any empirical-theoretical discrepancy as Monte Carlo variation unless assumptions are violated.
In [55]:
ns=[1,2,5,10,20,50,100,200]
R=6000
ks=[]
for n in ns:
    x=rng.exponential(scale=1,size=(R,n))
    z=np.sqrt(n)*(x.mean(axis=1)-1)
    ks.append(stats.kstest(z,'norm').statistic)
source=ColumnDataSource({'n':ns,'ks':ks})
p=figure(title='CLT convergence diagnostic',width=800,height=420,x_axis_type='log',
         x_axis_label='n',y_axis_label='KS statistic vs N(0,1)',
         tools='pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save')
r=p.line('n','ks',source=source,line_width=3)
p.scatter('n','ks',source=source,size=8)
p.add_tools(HoverTool(renderers=[r],tooltips=[('n','@n'),('KS','@ks{0.0000}')]))
show(p)

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The numerical output is a finite-sample approximation to the theoretical probability result. Small differences are expected.

When interpreting a simulation, always separate:

  • the theorem or exact formula,
  • the estimator used in the code,
  • finite-simulation error,
  • and the visual evidence.

19. Distribution Approximations¶

Approximations connect exact finite-sample distributions with limiting probability theory.

Approximations are model replacements¶

When replacing one distribution with another, always ask:

  1. What limiting argument justifies the replacement?
  2. Are the parameters in the required regime?
  3. Is the approximation being used in the centre or extreme tails?
  4. Is a continuity correction required?

An approximation can be excellent in one parameter regime and poor in another.

Scenario 19A — Normal approximation to Binomial¶

For suitable (n,p),

[ Binomial(n,p)\approx N(np,np(1-p)). ]

A continuity correction improves the approximation.

Approximation checklist¶

For a Binomial (X\sim Bin(n,p)), the Normal approximation is generally better when both

[ np ]

and

[ n(1-p) ]

are reasonably large.

The continuity correction compares discrete probability mass at integer (k) with Normal area from (k-0.5) to (k+0.5).

In [88]:
n,p0=100,0.35
mu=n*p0
sd=np.sqrt(n*p0*(1-p0))
x=np.arange(15,56)
exact=stats.binom.pmf(x,n,p0)
approx=stats.norm.cdf(x+0.5,mu,sd)-stats.norm.cdf(x-0.5,mu,sd)
show(line_plot(x,[exact,approx],['Exact Binomial','Normal approximation'],
               title='Normal approximation to Binomial(100,0.35)',x_label='k',y_label='Probability'))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The two curves are close because the chosen parameters are in an approximation-friendly regime. This is not guaranteed for every parameter choice.

Checkpoint: modify the parameters until the approximation visibly deteriorates. What assumption became weaker?

Scenario 19B — Poisson approximation to Binomial¶

For large (n), small (p), and (\lambda=np),

[ Binomial(n,p)\approx Poisson(\lambda). ]

Approximation checklist¶

The Poisson approximation works when:

  • (n) is large,
  • (p) is small,
  • (\lambda=np) remains moderate.

The Binomial models many rare opportunities; the Poisson emerges as the limiting count model for those rare events.

In [57]:
n,p0=1000,0.004
lam=n*p0
x=np.arange(15)
exact=stats.binom.pmf(x,n,p0)
approx=stats.poisson.pmf(x,lam)
show(line_plot(x,[exact,approx],['Exact Binomial','Poisson approximation'],
               title='Poisson approximation to Binomial',x_label='k',y_label='Probability'))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The two curves are close because the chosen parameters are in an approximation-friendly regime. This is not guaranteed for every parameter choice.

Checkpoint: modify the parameters until the approximation visibly deteriorates. What assumption became weaker?

20. Monte Carlo Estimation¶

Monte Carlo replaces an expectation with an empirical average:

[ E[g(X)]\approx\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ng(X_i). ]

This is a direct computational use of the Law of Large Numbers.

Monte Carlo = expectation computed by sampling¶

Many integrals can be written as expectations. Once we can sample from the relevant distribution, we estimate the expectation using an average.

[ E[g(X)] \approx \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ng(X_i). ]

The LLN gives consistency. The CLT often gives approximate uncertainty:

[ SE(\hat\mu)\approx \frac{s}{\sqrt N}. ]

This is the computational backbone of much of simulation-based statistics.

Scenario 20A — Monte Carlo integration¶

For (U\sim U(0,1)),

[ E[e^{-U^2}]=\int_0^1e^{-x^2},dx. ]

Turning an integral into an expectation¶

If (U\sim U(0,1)),

[ E[g(U)]¶

\int_0^1g(u),du. ]

Therefore numerical integration can be performed by averaging (g(U_i)) over random Uniform samples.

In [58]:
U=rng.uniform(0,1,800_000)
mc=np.mean(np.exp(-U**2))
exact,_=quad(lambda x:np.exp(-x*x),0,1)
pd.DataFrame({'method':['Monte Carlo','Numerical quadrature'],'estimate':[mc,exact]})
Out[58]:
method estimate
0 Monte Carlo 0.746765
1 Numerical quadrature 0.746824

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The numerical output is a finite-sample approximation to the theoretical probability result. Small differences are expected.

When interpreting a simulation, always separate:

  • the theorem or exact formula,
  • the estimator used in the code,
  • finite-simulation error,
  • and the visual evidence.

Scenario 20B — Monte Carlo convergence rate¶

The root-mean-square error typically scales as

[ N^{-1/2}. ]

Why the (N^{-1/2}) rate matters¶

If standard error is proportional to (1/\sqrt N):

  • 4× as many samples gives about 2× smaller error,
  • 100× as many samples gives about 10× smaller error.

This slow rate motivates variance-reduction techniques in advanced Monte Carlo methods.

In [59]:
true_value=np.pi
Ns=np.array([100,300,1000,3000,10000,30000])
reps=60
rmse=[]
for N in Ns:
    est=[]
    for _ in range(reps):
        x=rng.uniform(-1,1,N)
        y=rng.uniform(-1,1,N)
        est.append(4*np.mean(x*x+y*y<=1))
    est=np.array(est)
    rmse.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((est-true_value)**2)))
reference=rmse[0]*np.sqrt(Ns[0]/Ns)
show(line_plot(Ns,[rmse,reference],['Observed RMSE','Reference ∝ N^(-1/2)'],
               title='Monte Carlo convergence rate',x_label='N',y_label='RMSE'))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The numerical output is a finite-sample approximation to the theoretical probability result. Small differences are expected.

When interpreting a simulation, always separate:

  • the theorem or exact formula,
  • the estimator used in the code,
  • finite-simulation error,
  • and the visual evidence.

21. Inverse-Transform Sampling¶

If (U\sim U(0,1)), then

[ X=F^{-1}(U) ]

has CDF (F).

Inverse transform sampling step by step¶

To generate (X) with target CDF (F):

  1. Generate (U\sim U(0,1)).
  2. Set

[ X=F^{-1}(U). ]

Why it works:

[ P(F^{-1}(U)\le x)¶

P(U\le F(x))¶

F(x). ]

This is one of the cleanest bridges between probability theory and random-number generation.

Scenario 21A — Generate an Exponential variable manually¶

For the Exponential CDF,

[ X=-\frac{\ln(1-U)}{\lambda}. ]

Recognition pattern¶

Exponential models waiting time to the next event when events follow a constant-rate Poisson process.

Its constant hazard and memorylessness are two views of the same underlying lack-of-ageing property.

In [60]:
lam=1.4
U=rng.uniform(0,1,160_000)
X=-np.log(1-U)/lam
p=bokeh_hist(X,80,True,'Inverse-transform Exponential sampling','x')
grid=np.linspace(0,6,500)
p.line(grid,stats.expon.pdf(grid,scale=1/lam),line_width=3,legend_label='Target PDF')
show(p)

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The empirical histogram/PMF should approximate the theoretical distribution, with visible random fluctuation caused by finite sample size.

Focus on support, centre, spread, skewness, and tail behaviour rather than merely checking whether the lines overlap.

Checkpoint: identify which parameter controls location, spread, rate, or shape in this example.

Scenario 21B — Numerical inverse CDF for a Beta distribution¶

SciPy's ppf is the inverse CDF / quantile function.

Simulation logic¶

A Uniform variable represents a random percentile. Applying a target distribution's quantile function converts that percentile into the corresponding value on the target scale.

This makes (F^{-1}) a general-purpose probability-model generator.

In [61]:
a,b=2.5,5
U=rng.uniform(0,1,150_000)
X=stats.beta.ppf(U,a,b)
p=bokeh_hist(X,70,True,'Inverse-CDF sampling for Beta(2.5,5)','x')
grid=np.linspace(0.001,0.999,500)
p.line(grid,stats.beta.pdf(grid,a,b),line_width=3,legend_label='Beta PDF')
show(p)

Interpretation and takeaway¶

The empirical histogram/PMF should approximate the theoretical distribution, with visible random fluctuation caused by finite sample size.

Focus on support, centre, spread, skewness, and tail behaviour rather than merely checking whether the lines overlap.

Checkpoint: identify which parameter controls location, spread, rate, or shape in this example.

22. Sampling Distributions¶

A population distribution describes randomness in observations. A sampling distribution describes randomness in a statistic computed from repeated samples.

For Normal observations,

[ X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar X\sim N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). ]

Population distribution vs sampling distribution¶

A population distribution answers:

What can one observation (X) look like?

A sampling distribution answers:

If I repeatedly collect samples and compute a statistic (T), how does (T) vary?

For Normal data,

[ \bar X\sim N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) ]

exactly. More generally, the CLT often gives an approximate version of this result.

Scenario 22A — Sampling distribution of the sample mean¶

Two levels of randomness¶

Do not confuse the individual observations with the statistic.

One run: [ X_1,\ldots,X_n \longrightarrow \bar X. ]

Repeated runs: [ \bar X^{(1)},\bar X^{(2)},\ldots ]

The distribution across those repeated (\bar X)'s is the sampling distribution.

In [62]:
mu,sd=5,2
R=10000
plots=[]
for n in [4,25,100]:
    means=rng.normal(mu,sd,size=(R,n)).mean(axis=1)
    p=bokeh_hist(means,60,True,f'Sampling distribution of mean, n={n}','sample mean')
    grid=np.linspace(mu-3*sd/np.sqrt(n),mu+3*sd/np.sqrt(n),500)
    p.line(grid,stats.norm.pdf(grid,mu,sd/np.sqrt(n)),line_width=3,legend_label='Exact theory')
    plots.append(p)
show(column(*plots))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

Increasing sample size stabilises averages because independent deviations are increasingly averaged out. The individual observations remain random; what becomes stable is the aggregate.

Checkpoint: state the difference between convergence of the sample mean and convergence of the underlying observations.

Scenario 22B — Variance of the sample mean shrinks as (1/n)¶

[ Var(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}. ]

Student workflow¶

Before running the code:

  1. identify the random experiment,
  2. state the relevant random variable/event,
  3. write the theoretical quantity being estimated,
  4. predict the qualitative plot shape,
  5. run the simulation,
  6. explain any empirical-theoretical discrepancy as Monte Carlo variation unless assumptions are violated.
In [63]:
ns=np.array([2,5,10,20,50,100,200])
R=8000
emp_var=[]
for n in ns:
    means=rng.normal(0,3,size=(R,n)).mean(axis=1)
    emp_var.append(means.var())
theory=9/ns
show(line_plot(ns,[emp_var,theory],['Empirical Var(mean)','Theory σ²/n'],
               title='Variance of the sample mean',x_label='n',y_label='Variance'))

Interpretation and takeaway¶

Increasing sample size stabilises averages because independent deviations are increasingly averaged out. The individual observations remain random; what becomes stable is the aggregate.

Checkpoint: state the difference between convergence of the sample mean and convergence of the underlying observations.

23. Common Conceptual Traps¶

1. PDF value is not a point probability¶

For continuous (X), (P(X=x)=0) even if (f_X(x)>0).

2. Zero correlation is not independence¶

The (Y=X^2) example demonstrated this directly.

3. Mutual exclusivity is not independence¶

Positive-probability mutually exclusive events are necessarily dependent.

4. Conditional probability is directional¶

Usually,

[ P(A\mid B)\ne P(B\mid A). ]

5. LLN and CLT assumptions matter¶

Heavy-tailed distributions can violate finite-mean or finite-variance assumptions.

6. Simulation is evidence, not proof¶

A simulation can illustrate a theorem or find a counterexample, but it cannot replace a mathematical proof.

24. Relevance to Data Science and Machine Learning¶

ST2131 concepts appear almost everywhere in statistical ML.

  • Bernoulli / Binomial: binary classification and conversion rates.
  • Bayes: Naive Bayes and Bayesian posterior updating.
  • Conditional distributions: predictive modelling targets (P(Y\mid X)).
  • Expectation: expected risk and loss functions.
  • Covariance: multivariate Gaussian models and PCA foundations.
  • LLN: empirical averages approximate population expectations.
  • CLT: approximate sampling distributions and uncertainty quantification.
  • Monte Carlo: Bayesian inference and simulation-based algorithms.
  • Change of variables: inverse-CDF methods and normalising flows.

25. Exercises and Extension Scenarios¶

Exercise 1 — Birthday paradox¶

Compare 365, 366 and 100 equally likely categories. Explain how the collision threshold changes.

Exercise 2 — Medical testing¶

Use prevalence 1%, sensitivity 99%, specificity 99%. Compute (P(D\mid +)) and explain why it is not 99%.

Exercise 3 — Hypergeometric vs Binomial¶

Increase population size while keeping the success fraction and sample size fixed. Measure the maximum PMF difference.

Exercise 4 — Memorylessness¶

Verify it for Geometric and Exponential. Show it fails for Gamma(shape=3).

Exercise 5 — Transformation¶

Let (X\sim U(0,1)) and (Y=-\log X). Derive and simulate the distribution of (Y).

Exercise 6 — Covariance¶

Construct dependent examples with positive, negative and zero covariance.

Exercise 7 — Law of total expectation¶

Build a two-group mixture model and verify (E[X]=E[E[X\mid G]]).

Exercise 8 — Law of total variance¶

Verify

[ Var(Y)=E[Var(Y\mid X)]+Var(E[Y\mid X]). ]

Exercise 9 — CLT speed¶

Compare Uniform, Exponential, Bernoulli and Lognormal populations using the KS statistic.

Exercise 10 — Heavy tails¶

Compare sample averages for Cauchy and Pareto distributions with different shape parameters.

Exercise 11 — Monte Carlo precision¶

Estimate (\pi) at different sample sizes and confirm RMSE scales approximately as (N^{-1/2}).

Exercise 12 — Approximation failure¶

Find parameter regimes where Normal-to-Binomial and Poisson-to-Binomial approximations become poor.

Exercise 13 — Order statistics¶

For IID (U(0,1)), simulate the maximum and verify

[ E[M_n]=\frac{n}{n+1}. ]

Exercise 14 — Rare-event simulation¶

Estimate a rare Normal tail probability with naive Monte Carlo and importance sampling. Compare estimator variance.

Exercise 15 — Beta-Binomial Bayesian update¶

Start with a Beta prior, observe Bernoulli data sequentially, and use Bokeh to plot posterior density after 1, 10, 50 and 200 observations.

26. Final ST2131 Mental Model¶

A useful dependency chain is

[ \text{Counting} \rightarrow \text{Events} \rightarrow \text{Conditioning} \rightarrow \text{Random Variables} \rightarrow \text{Distributions} ]

followed by

[ \text{Joint Distributions} \rightarrow \text{Conditional Expectation} \rightarrow \text{Covariance} \rightarrow \text{Transforms / MGFs} \rightarrow \text{LLN / CLT}. ]

Revision priority¶

  1. Conditional probability and Bayes
  2. PMF / PDF / CDF
  3. Discrete and continuous distributions
  4. Joint, marginal and conditional distributions
  5. Expectation, variance and covariance
  6. Conditional expectation
  7. Transformations
  8. MGFs
  9. Probability inequalities
  10. LLN
  11. CLT and distribution approximations

If you can explain why each arrow in the concept chain is necessary, rather than merely memorising formulas, you have understood the backbone of ST2131.

27. Methodical ST2131 Problem-Solving Framework¶

Use this as a final exam checklist.

A. Finite counting problems¶

  1. Define the elementary outcome.
  2. Decide ordered vs unordered.
  3. Decide replacement vs no replacement.
  4. Count the sample space.
  5. Count the favourable set.
  6. Verify equal likelihood before taking a ratio.
  7. Consider the complement for “at least one” questions.

B. Conditional probability / Bayes problems¶

  1. Identify the conditioning direction.
  2. Write (P(A\mid B)) in words.
  3. Partition the population if multiple sources/groups exist.
  4. Compute evidence with total probability.
  5. Apply Bayes only after the denominator is clear.
  6. Sanity-check against the prior.

C. Distribution-recognition problems¶

Ask:

  • fixed number of trials or fixed time interval?
  • binary outcomes?
  • independent trials?
  • with or without replacement?
  • count or waiting time?
  • continuous positive waiting time?
  • support restricted to ([0,1])?
  • additive measurement variation?

Then choose the distribution.

D. Expectation and variance¶

  1. Identify PMF/PDF.
  2. Check support carefully.
  3. Compute expectation.
  4. Compute (E[X^2]).
  5. Use

[ Var(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2. ]

  1. For sums, check covariance before adding variances.

E. Joint distributions¶

  1. Identify joint support.
  2. Verify total probability integrates/sums to 1.
  3. Marginalise by integrating/summing out unwanted variables.
  4. Condition by dividing joint by marginal.
  5. Test independence via factorisation.

F. Transformations¶

  1. Find the transformed support.
  2. Invert (y=g(x)).
  3. Differentiate the inverse.
  4. Apply absolute Jacobian.
  5. Verify normalisation.

G. LLN / CLT¶

Before applying either theorem, state its assumptions.

  • LLN answers whether averages stabilise.
  • CLT answers the approximate shape of rescaled sampling error.
  • Neither theorem justifies ignoring heavy-tail pathologies automatically.

28. Final Self-Test¶

You should be able to answer these without code.

  1. Why is a PDF value not a probability?
  2. Why does (P(A\mid B)\neq P(B\mid A)) in general?
  3. Why are mutually exclusive positive-probability events dependent?
  4. Give an example of dependent but uncorrelated variables.
  5. Why does Hypergeometric sampling differ from Binomial sampling?
  6. Why is the Exponential distribution memoryless?
  7. Explain marginalisation without using a formula.
  8. Explain conditional expectation as a function.
  9. Why does covariance appear in (Var(X+Y))?
  10. Explain convolution as “all ways to make a sum.”
  11. What does an MGF buy us?
  12. Why can Markov/Chebyshev bounds be loose?
  13. State the LLN in plain English.
  14. State the CLT in plain English.
  15. Why does increasing (n) not make raw observations Normal?
  16. When can a Normal approximation to Binomial fail?
  17. Why does Monte Carlo accuracy improve only like (1/\sqrt N)?
  18. Why is Cauchy a useful counterexample?
  19. What is a sampling distribution?
  20. How does ST2131 probability become the foundation of statistical inference?

If you can explain each answer in your own words and then support it mathematically, you have moved beyond formula memorisation.
